data.title: Fortified settlements of the Otomani culture in eastern Slovakia
data.excerpt: Five fortified settlements of the Otomani (Otomani–Füzesabony) culture are compared here: Nižná Myšľa, Košice – Barca and Rozhanovce in the Košice Basin, Spišský Štvrtok in the Spiš region and Trzcinica in the Polish Carpathians. The paper traces their earthen ramparts, ditches and gateways and the systematic rows of huts inside them, and asks whether these Early Bronze Age centres were the first proto-urban settlement units in the territory of present-day Slovakia.

timeline.title: Rescue excavation at Barca
timeline.description: Gravel extraction destroyed part of the settlement, so a rescue operation was carried out from 1952 to 1954; it could not investigate the whole site.

timeline.title: Excavation at Spišský Štvrtok
timeline.description: Because the occupation layers were being intensively ploughed, a systematic rescue excavation took place from 1968 to 1974 and investigated the entire area of the fortified settlement (6,600 m²).

timeline.title: Excavation at Rozhanovce
timeline.description: A rescue excavation took place at the site from 1978 to 1980 and succeeded in uncovering part of the fortified settlement.

timeline.title: First stage of excavation at Trzcinica
timeline.description: Systematic excavations at the Polish site of Trzcinica took place from 1991 to 1997.

timeline.title: Second stage of excavation at Trzcinica
timeline.description: Excavations at the site of Trzcinica continued from 2005 to 2009.

children.text: INTRODUCTION AND AIM OF THE PAPER

Given the availability of sources and published literature, the paper focuses on the fortified settlements of the Otomani or Otomani–Füzesabony culture, or complex. In total I describe and compare in more detail the situation at five hillforts (Fig. 1). From eastern Slovakia, from the Košice Basin, these are specifically the fortified settlements at Nižná Myšľa, Košice – Barca and Rozhanovce. From the Spiš region, the site of Spišský Štvrtok. I have also included in the paper the fortified settlement of Trzcinica, from the Polish part of the Carpathians, with noticeable Otomani elements.
The aim of the paper is to characterise the fortified settlements of the region and to observe their basic characteristics.

For the purposes of the paper I have compiled a catalogue, on which the following text is based. In the catalogue I first give, for each fortified settlement, basic information about its location, area, state of research and the extent to which the site has been investigated. I then report on the origin of the Otomani settlement, the number of horizons and its subsequent demise. Next I characterise the type of fortification, the internal structure and the built-up layout. The catalogue of sites is appended to the paper, and therefore the information on the individual fortified settlements that derives from it is not cited in more detail in the text itself.

children.text: For the sake of objectivity, and in order to summarise and clarify the data on the origin, duration and phases of the individual hillforts, I have evaluated the information from the available sources and created a chronological table, which I have also linked to the text and to the catalogue and present in the appendix (Tab. I). For completeness I also include further illustrations, which I cite both in the text and in the catalogue itself.

In the following section I first briefly outline the basic chronology of the Otomani culture in eastern Slovakia. I then sketch the origin, development and demise of the fortified settlements in the region from both a chronological and a chorological point of view. I generalise the information on location and area and also consider the wider hinterland of the settlements. Next I characterise in general terms the manner of fortification and the types of gateway. I assess the internal structure of the settlements and the area and character of the houses (huts). In conclusion I present possible interpretations relating to the existence of the fortified settlements from the point of view of contemporary society.

children.text: CHRONOLOGY AND DISTRIBUTION

The Otomani culture in eastern Slovakia develops on the basis of the Košťany culture and is divided into three basic stages: the initial – Košťany–Otomani stage, and the classical Otomani stage, which is further divided into an earlier and a later phase. The final stage is already connected with the so-called Koszider horizon (Tab. I; Furmánek/Veliačik/Vladár 1991, 82, 84).

The territory of the Otomani culture was extensive. It is assumed that its original area of distribution was the Tisza region and the north-eastern part of Romania. From the territory of Slovakia the oldest more numerous finds are known from the Košice Basin, from the transition of phases BA1/BA2 (approximately 2000 cal. B.C.). Eastern Slovakia, together with the adjoining part of Poland, which the Otomani culture reaches at its peak, forms the northernmost sphere of its distribution (Tab. I; Furmánek/Veliačik/Vladár 1991, 82, 84).
THE ORIGIN, DEVELOPMENT AND DEMISE OF THE FORTIFIED SETTLEMENTS IN THE REGION

To understand better the origin of the fortified settlements one has to look at the culture as a whole and at the situation in several regions. The fact is that the emergence of fortified settlements in eastern Slovakia is connected with the gradual development and geographical expansion of the culture. At the same time the fortified settlements are understandably a certain indicator of cultural development and advancement. Through gradual development the culture consolidates and crystallises, until at the beginning of its middle stage the first fortified settlements begin to appear in the Košice Basin, specifically at Nižná Myšľa and Barca (Tab. I).

In the course of further development the fortified settlement at Rozhanovce comes into being, still in the earlier phase of the middle stage, and the culture also moves into further areas. Specifically into the Spiš region, where the fortified settlement at Spišský Štvrtok arises towards the end of the later phase (Tab. I).

In the later phase of the middle stage the development of the fortified settlements and of the culture itself reaches its peak. Apparently thanks to favourable living conditions and to its internal situation, the culture expands further and crosses the Carpathians as far as Poland, where the fortified settlement of Trzcinica with numerous Otomani finds lies (Fig. 1, Tab. I).

The demise and decline of the fortified settlements is relatively sudden. At the end of the later stage the culture begins to stagnate and the individual fortified settlements gradually come to an end. The Otomani complex in eastern Slovakia breaks up and survives only at a local level (Tab. I). Opinions on the demise of the Otomani culture differ in Central European scholarship. The connection is to be sought in the change of the historical situation at the transition of phases BB1/BB2 (Vladár 2012, 390)

For example, the settlement at Spišský Štvrtok came to an end suddenly in a great fire, after which, however, parts of the population continued to live there. Sudden destruction horizons can also be observed at other sites, for example at Barca. Depending on the region, later cultures develop partly out of the Otomani culture and partly under new influences. Continuity is documented, for example, by the surviving lunula-shaped pendants (Vladár 2012, 390-392). In the case of the fortified settlement of Trzcinica, J. Gancarski reckons with a further development of the Otomani culture as late as phase BD, during which the settlement itself also grows larger (Fig. 9; Gancarski 2011, Ryc. 31).
LOCATION, AREA AND HINTERLAND OF THE SETTLEMENTS

In terms of location, all cases involve elevated positions close to rivers and streams. They are mostly described as terraces, and in the case of Barca and Spišský Štvrtok also as promontory positions projecting into flat terrain (after Furmánek/Veliačik/Vladár 1991, 181). Since these were elevated positions, the steep slope often improved the possibilities of defence. The placing of the settlements was also deliberate because of the presence of routes running along the river beds. For example, the settlement at Nižná Myšľa lay at the confluence of as many as three rivers, the Hornád, the Torysa and the Olšava. The settlement at Rozhanovce lay by the river Torysa, on the link between the Košice Basin and the Šariš region. In general it can be stated that each of the fortified sites lay in an advantageous strategic position.

children.text: It is not entirely possible to answer the question of the area of the settlements in all cases. In most cases only the size of the fortified enclosure can be estimated more precisely, and the question of the hinterland remains open. The size of the fortified part ranged from 3,200 m² at Rozhanovce up to a presumed 10,000 m² in the first phase of the settlement at Nižná Myšľa. In the second phase at Nižná Myšľa the settlement reaches an area of as much as 70,000 m², which, however, is apparently connected with some marked change in the social situation, since the enlargement of the enclosure also damaged and disregarded the earlier cemetery.

The fortified settlements were part of a wider whole, or rather of a pattern of occupation, as is also documented by surveys in their surroundings (Nižná Myšľa, Rozhanovce). In terms of location and area they cannot have been places of refuge. Taking into account also the further structure, which I discuss below, and the concentration of specific finds, the settlements were apparently a kind of regional centre. A narrower hinterland outside the enclosure belonged to the fortified settlement, and probably also further unfortified settlements in the vicinity.
FORTIFICATIONS AND GATEWAYS

The system of fortification of the settlements was related to the character of the terrain. Understandably, in places where there was a steep drop it was not necessary to build a massive rampart. This can be seen well on the plans from Spišský Štvrtok and Trzcinica (Fig. 7, 9). In the case of the settlement at Spišský Štvrtok only a stone wall was built in these places, which then joined the rampart (Fig. 8).

Conversely, in places where access was relatively easy it was necessary to secure and fortify the settlement appropriately. At Spišský Štvrtok a massive rampart with a ditch protected the more accessible eastern side (Fig. 7). At Trzcinica a ditch was likewise built in addition to the rampart in the most accessible part of the terrain (Fig. 9). A similar situation can be observed at the other fortified settlements. In all cases the fortification consisted of an earthen rampart and a ditch, that is, it was built simply from the available resources. The material obtained in digging the ditch was used to pile up the rampart. The rampart was commonly strengthened with a post construction (for example at Barca) and had a palisade on top (Spišský Štvrtok). Defensibility could also be increased by the presence of rivers and streams (Barca, Rozhanovce), which, apart from the steep drops of their beds, also made the terrain harder to access.

blocks.caption: Fig. 3 – Schematic plan of the settlement at Barca I (after Kabát 1955, 595, fig. 259).
blocks.alt: Fig. 3 – Schematic plan of the settlement at Barca I (after Kabát 1955, 595, fig. 259).

children.text: While the fortifications of the enclosures were of a similar character, in the case of the entrance to the hillfort different types of gateway are involved. At Nižná Myšľa a narrow gateway with a bridge over the ditch. At Spišský Štvrtok a gateway with bastions (Fig. 7), and in the case of Trzcinica an inturned pincer-shaped entrance. At Nižná Myšľa and Trzcinica the gateways themselves undoubtedly had good defensive qualities. Remarkable is the gateway at Spišský Štvrtok, whose entrance is considerably wide. In the area of the gateway, however, there were also houses, which apparently served a defensive function as well and made access more difficult (Fig. 7).
INTERNAL STRUCTURE

At most of the fortified settlements studied it proved possible to identify a systematic built-up layout. The huts were deliberately oriented next to one another, for example in rows (Nižná Myšľa, Barca, Rozhanovce). The row layout and the evident streets can be seen well on the plan from Barca. The houses stand about half a metre apart and the street is roughly 2.5 metres wide (Fig. 3).

The arrangement of the houses was not random in the case of Spišský Štvrtok either. Although, as the plan of the hillfort shows, the houses did not stand in rows, they were concentrated and arranged in a certain way within the enclosure (Fig. 7). In the north-western part J. Vladár assumes the existence of an acropolis, that is, a place where the elite, or rather the higher-ranking inhabitants, resided. He concludes this partly because of the supposedly different character of the houses, but mainly on the basis of the density of hoards. Specifically, in feature 5/68 several gold and bronze objects and items of jewellery were found in as many as three places (Vladár 2012, 383). The claim is also supported by the spatial relationship of the acropolis to the gateway and to the rest of the settlement (Fig. 7). At Spišský Štvrtok traces of roads paved with stones were also found.

At some fortified settlements the presence of huts close to the rampart, or rather to the fortification, is interesting. At Nižná Myšľa, for example, the houses follow the line of the rampart. At Barca, by contrast, there was an open space or a street more than 2 metres wide between the houses and the rampart (Fig. 3). At Spišský Štvrtok, in the western part of the settlement, a stone wall formed one of the longer walls of the houses (Fig. 7).

On the basis of the information above I conclude that the huts may have been placed next to the fortification because this made construction simpler (Spišský Štvrtok). It is possible that huts close to the fortification also improved its defensibility, if we disregard the fact that in an attack they could easily catch fire and damage the structure of the fortification or any palisade. Which, apart from a possible street, may also be the reason why there is an open space between the rampart and the huts in the case of Barca.

blocks.alt: Fig. 4 – Sequence of layers at Barca I (after Kabát 1955, 597, fig. 260).

children.text: Fires were generally frequent at the fortified settlements. Sometimes the houses were rebuilt on their original sites (Barca), but a change in the urban layout could also occur (Točík 1994, 59-61). Thanks to the fires it is possible to distinguish different layers, that is, phases of the settlement (Fig. 4), between which rebuildings can be traced. The main phases of the individual settlements are marked in the chronological table (Tab. I).
HUTS, HOUSES

The size of the huts ranged roughly from 20 m² to 55 m². They were one-, two- or three-roomed huts. The most frequently occurring was the single-roomed house with an area of 20 m² (Nižná Myšľa, Rozhanovce). It usually had a square or slightly rectangular plan (Fig. 6). The houses were commonly of log or post construction with daubed walls and a presumed gabled roof. A hearth was located in the rooms.

The variety of the houses was well documented in the case of the fortified settlement at Barca. Huts of various dimensions with different internal divisions were uncovered. In terms of spatial division, all 3 types of hut mentioned above were represented at the site. The largest dwelling feature whose dimensions are mentioned in the literature on the sites is the three-roomed house no. 3 from Barca, measuring 12.5 and 4.5 metres, which amounts to approximately 55 m² (Fig. 5).

Apart from their primary residential function, in the case of Spišský Štvrtok some houses may, according to J. Vladár, have served as specialised production workshops. In these houses unfinished metal products and other objects connected with metal casting were found (Vladár 2012, 383, 384).

blocks.caption: Fig. 5 – The fortified settlement at Spišský Štvrtok – Myšia Hôrka 1 – the floor of a hut and a street (after Kabát 1955, 613, fig. 287);
blocks.alt: Fig. 5 – The fortified settlement at Spišský Štvrtok – Myšia Hôrka 1 – the floor of a hut and a street (after Kabát 1955, 613, fig. 287);

children.text: In the case of the three-roomed house no. 3 at Barca, J. Kabát considers a division of the interior into a kitchen, storage rooms and a bedroom. The middle room, which had no hearth and whose floor was probably lined with wooden rods about 5 cm wide, is thought to have served as a store. The other rooms had a daubed and fired floor and contained hearths (Fig. 5; Kabát 1955; 596, 597).
CONCLUSION

In the Early Bronze Age we encounter fortified settlements across a wider Central European territory. The fortified settlements of the Otomani culture were the first settlements of this kind in eastern Slovakia. The very fact that they came into being documents a certain social advancement. The ingenious system of fortification of the settlements, the systematic built-up layout and the number of specific finds only confirm this.

In assessing the significance of the fortified settlements one must bear in mind that, because of their strategic position and their area, they were natural centres with a wider hinterland. The evidence of fortification indicates a need for defence and implies the dominance of the settlement in the surrounding terrain. The presence of fortification also suggests that some kind of military component may have been based there. The systematic built-up layout points to the fact that someone must have governed, or at least directed, that society.

blocks.caption: 2 – the floor of hut no. 3 divided into 3 rooms (after Kabát 1955, 599, fig. 261).
blocks.alt: 2 – the floor of hut no. 3 divided into 3 rooms (after Kabát 1955, 599, fig. 261).

children.text: Various offerings, votive hoards and cult features (Spišský Štvrtok, Nižná Myšľa), but also some artefacts, could be regarded as evidence of cult practices taking place within the settlements. Finds of unfinished metal products indicate a concentration of the metal-casting craft (Spišský Štvrtok). At the same time, other less demanding branches of production were understandably present in the area of the settlement.

Further questions, which I only outline in conclusion, are the extent of the territory that belonged to a particular fortified settlement; whether stores of grain were kept at the fortified settlements and in what way the farming hinterland belonging to a settlement, or the other unfortified settlements in the vicinity, corresponded to it. One can also consider possible distant contacts and impulses that may have influenced the development and appearance of the Otomani fortified settlements.

Not entirely clear and resolved is the relatively sudden demise of the settlements, whether they came to an end because of internal strife or with the arrival of new cultures that disrupted the structure of the hillforts of the Otomani culture (Vladár 2012).

blocks.caption: Fig. 6 – Plans of a dwelling at Rozhanovce (after Gašaj 1983, 131, fig. 1).
blocks.alt: Fig. 6 – Plans of a dwelling at Rozhanovce (after Gašaj 1983, 131, fig. 1).

children.text: From the paper it can be summarised that at the fortified settlements, as centres of the given region, all the most important activities of an economic, social and also spiritual character were concentrated. In their case one has to reckon with a concentration of various population groups and of a kind of higher stratum, as is suggested by finds of valuable objects and also by some of the graves at Nižná Myšľa. On the basis of the study I conclude that the fortified settlements of the Early Bronze Age are a civilisational phenomenon that can be regarded as the first proto-urban or higher-order settlement units in the territory of present-day Slovakia.
CATALOGUE OF SITES
Nižná Myšľa – Varhegy (Olexa 2003)
Location, area and state of research

The site is located on a widened terrace on the left bank of the Hornád, above the confluence of the Torysa and the Olšava. The junction of the rivers was undoubtedly an important crossroads, where trade routes also met in the past (Olexa 2003, 19).

children.text: A systematic excavation has been under way at the site at Nižná Myšľa since 1977. The area of the fortified settlements and the contemporary cemetery are being investigated. Of the estimated size of the site, 10 ha, about a third has been investigated so far (Olexa 2003, 10).
Chronology – the origin of the settlement, the number of horizons and its demise

In terms of occupation, the development at the site is sharply determined by two different fortified settlements. While the duration of the first is estimated at as much as 200 years, the existence of the second is delimited by only about fifty years. The origin of the first settlement is placed at the beginning of the earlier stage of the classical phase of the Otomani culture. The second settlement arises immediately after the first, at the end of the later classical horizon (Tab. I; Olexa 2003, 49, 50).
The settlement complex, fortification, internal layout and features

At Nižná Myšľa a cemetery lies in the immediate vicinity of the fortified settlements and is directly connected with their development. Extensive excavation shows that the fortified settlements formed a hinterland for the wider surroundings (Olexa 2003, 9).

The first settlement, with an area of about one hectare, shows signs of a systematic built-up layout, with the streets slightly raised above the level of the houses. The lines of houses regularly followed the arc of the fortification, which consisted of a wide ditch 6 metres deep and an earthen bank, or rather a rampart. The rampart was 8 to 10 metres wide, piled up with the earth obtained in digging the ditch. In the eastern section the bank was interrupted by an entrance gateway, to which a bridge across the ditch apparently led. The gateway had a timber-and-stone construction (Olexa 2003, 41-43).

In the case of the second fortress an area of as much as 7 hectares is assumed, and the settlement was completely reorganised. The construction of the new settlement did not respect the old cemetery, across which new features and part of the fortification were built. The houses were rectangular, with an area of about 20 m². They partly show signs of a systematic built-up layout; some of them were built next to one another, about half a metre apart along their broader wall. In the phase of the second settlement a cult pit was also found (Olexa 2003, 49, 50).

The finds from the site testify to extensive agricultural and craft production: specifically, finds of raw materials and of semi-finished products for manufacture, and the character of some of the features (Olexa 2003, 43, 45, 47).
The fortified settlement at Barca I (Kabát 1955, Točík 1994)
Location, area and state of research

The fortified settlement at Barca lay on a 12-metre-high elevation created by the river Hornád. Gravel extraction destroyed part of the settlement and therefore it could not be investigated in its entirety by the rescue operation in 1952 to 1954 (Fig. 3; Kabát 1955, 594).
Chronology – the origin of the settlement, the number of horizons and its demise

In the case of the settlement at Barca, scholars' opinions differ on the dating of the individual layers, their overall chronological classification and their final number. A. Točík (1994) pointed out the divergence of opinions and offered further possibilities for interpreting the layers reported (Fig. 4).

Generally speaking, it could be said that in the case of the settlement at Barca 3 phases, or rather building horizons, can be discerned. The first horizon represents occupation with clay houses and a rampart, which can be dated, after synchronisation with the other sites, to phase BA2 (Tab. I). It is probably followed immediately by a second horizon with houses rebuilt on their original sites (Kabát 1955, 595, 596). A third occupation horizon was also recorded at the site, but no more precise evidence of features has survived from it (Točík 1994, 61).

According to A. Točík, the plan of the settlement with its systematic built-up layout does not come from a single phase, which is supposedly indicated by the failure of further houses to respect the road. He likewise speaks, however, of 3 chronological horizons of the settlement, the last of which he relates to the hoards at the site (Tab. I; Točík 1994, 59, 61).
The settlement complex, fortification, internal layout and features

The originally fortified settlement had an outer rampart 7 m in diameter, with an outer berm about 2 m wide between the rampart and the ditch. The rampart was strengthened with a post construction on both its inner and its outer face (Točík 1994, 59, 60).

In total, 23 houses in four rows were recorded by the excavation. On the plan of the settlement, traces of a systematic built-up layout are clearly visible. The huts were concentrated in rows mostly running north – south, apart from four houses in the east oriented at right angles, running east – west. They stood roughly half a metre apart along their longer side, and the shorter side faced the street, which was about 2.5 metres wide (Fig. 3; Kabát 1955, 600, 617).

In the case of particular houses a spatial division can be observed. Altogether they could be divided into 3 types: one-, two- and three-roomed. In the case of the three-roomed house no. 3, 12.5 metres long and 4.5 metres wide, J. Kabát considers a division into a kitchen, storage rooms and a bedroom (Fig. 5; Kabát 1955; 596, 597).
Rozhanovce – Plebanské II (Hôrka) (Gašaj 1983)
Location, area and state of research
The site lies on a strategically advantageous terrace in the valley of the river Torysa, which is the link between the Košice Basin and the Prešov–Šariš region.

A rescue excavation took place at the site in 1978 to 1980, which succeeded in uncovering part of the fortified settlement. Only the north-eastern part of the settlement, with an area of 800 m², was investigated. The total area of the inner enclosure was about 3,200 m². The excavation provided more detailed information on the fortification and on the internal layout of the settlement (Gašaj 1983, 130, 132).

children.text: Chronology – the origin of the settlement, the number of horizons and its demise

At Rozhanovce it proved possible to distinguish two occupation horizons of the Otomani culture. The author synchronises the beginning of the first with layer II/2 at Barca I. As further finds show, the first horizon, which came to an end in a fire, was immediately followed by a second occupation horizon (Tab. I; Gašaj 1983, 134).
The settlement complex, fortification, internal layout and features

The settlement at Rozhanovce is distinguished by a thorough fortification system. Given the character of the terrain, it was sufficient to fortify only the northern and eastern sides. The fortification consisted of a massive earthen rampart and an arc-shaped ditch. Defensibility was probably increased by the watercourse of the Torysa and, on the southern side, by the Olčkársky stream (Gašaj 1983, 130).

In total 17 features were found at Rozhanovce. The first occupation horizon from the investigated area is represented by 3 features, which, however, cannot be placed more precisely within the layout. The construction of the fortification apparently began already in the first horizon, but was not completed. The earthen rampart strengthened with a palisade, and the ditch, were not finished until the second horizon (Gašaj 1983, 132).

blocks.caption: Fig. 8 – Spišský Štvrtok - an attempted reconstruction of the situation in the south-eastern part of the site, where the stone wall joins the fortification system (after Vladár 1975, 19, fig. 3).
blocks.alt: Fig. 8 – Spišský Štvrtok - an attempted reconstruction of the situation in the south-eastern part of the site, where the stone wall joins the fortification system (after Vladár 1975, 19, fig. 3).

children.text: The finds from the later horizon point to a systematic internal layout. Seven huts were situated about 1 to 2 metres from the inner edge of the fortification. A further 4 huts were identified towards the interior of the settlement, and they point to a row layout with clear streets running at right angles to the palisade. Given the extent of the investigated area and of the total fortified area, roughly 40 features can be assumed in horizon 2. The later horizon, like the earlier one, came to an end in a fire, after which the site was no longer occupied during the Otomani culture (Gašaj 1983, 132, 134).

blocks.alt: Fortified settlements of the Otomani culture in eastern Slovakia

children.text: All the dwellings investigated so far were of the same character. They are rectangular single-roomed huts with approximately equal side lengths of 4.5 × 4.5 metres. The walls were daubed with clay. A hearth was located in the huts, in the centre or in a corner (Fig. 6; 131, 132).

Surveys and further excavations point to a wider hinterland of the settlement. According to D. Gašaj, the Olčkársky stream probably separated the inner enclosure from the farming part of the settlement to the south (Gašaj 1983, 130).
Spišský Štvrtok – Myšia hôrka (Vladár 1975)
Location, area and state of research
The settlement is situated in a place that has a natural fall from south to north, while the western part drops steeply into the valley through which the Machalovský stream flows (Vladár 1975, 4, 5).

Because the occupation layers were being intensively ploughed, a systematic rescue excavation took place at the site in 1968–1974 which, owing to the uniqueness of the finds, eventually investigated the entire area of the fortified settlement, 6,600 m² in total (Vladár 1975, 3, 4).
Chronology – the origin of the settlement, the number of horizons and its demise

In the case of the settlement at Spišský Štvrtok it proved possible to identify 2 occupation horizons. The earlier was represented only by less numerous finds in the north-eastern part. The second horizon was represented across the whole area of the hillfort. It arises in the classical phase and may partly persist until the final phase of the Otomani culture (Tab. I; Vladár 1975, 11-14).
The settlement complex, fortification, internal layout and features

The fortification system was adapted to the terrain. On the western side of the enclosure, where there is a steep fall, there was only a stone wall, which then joined the massive rampart with a ditch on the east (Fig. 8). A specific feature of this fortified settlement is the division of the rampart in the middle, with fairly massive bastions built on each of the two sides (Fig. 7). The total height of the rampart reached 6 metres. The rampart had an 80 cm wide wall-walk and traces of a palisade were also found on it (Vladár 1975, 4-6).

In terms of the internal layout of the settlement, no precise urban plan was recognised. In the north-eastern area the houses adjoined the stone wall along their longer side, and the wall at the same time formed one of their sides. In this part J. Vladár also assumes an acropolis, on the basis of the different character of the houses and the concentration of specific finds (Vladár 1975, 6-9). Traces of roads paved with stones were also recorded within the enclosure. One of the features was interpreted as a sacrificial site. It was a sunken pit located opposite the acropolis, near the gateway (Vladár 1975, 10).

A large number of artefacts, features and other indirect evidence pointing to varied craft production was also found at the settlement. The excavation also suggests that the hillfort was of regional importance and that a further farming hinterland belonged to it (Vladár 1975, 6-9).
Trzcinica – Karpacka Troja (Gancarski 2011)
Location, area and state of research

The site of Trzcinica lies on an elevated position created by the river Ropa. The position was used in several periods. Systematic excavations at the site took place mainly in 1991–1997 and 2005–2009. An area of about 1,900 m² was investigated (Gancarski 2011, 9, 14).

From the period of the Otomani culture comes only the upper part of the whole position, with an area of about 8,000 m² according to the plan. The other parts were used and fortified only later, in the Middle Ages (Fig. 9; Gancarski 2011, 15).

children.text: Chronology – the origin of the settlement, the number of horizons and its demise

At the beginning of the Bronze Age the area of the hillfort was occupied by the people of the Pleszów group. The influence of the Otomani culture gradually increases and from phase BB1 one can speak of its first phase. Occupation at the site persists even after the demise of the hillforts in Slovakia, with surviving Otomani elements (Gancarski 2011, 49, 50).
The settlement complex, fortification, internal layout and features

From the period of the Otomani culture a rampart 1.8–2.5 metres wide and about 1.1 metres high, with a palisade on top, is documented. A road, a pincer-shaped gateway and the fortification ditch were uncovered at the site. Several remains of burnt timbers and traces of houses were also found. The presence of bearers of the Otomani culture is documented by several similar artefacts also found in Slovakia (Gancarski 2011, 51-53).
